name: Rosa Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the drill crew at a big iron ore mine, fly-in fly-out, which means I fly up for eight days and home for six. I drive one blast-hole drill myself, the rig that bores the holes the explosives go into, and I watch two driverless drills on a tablet in my cab. If one of them hits hard rock or loses its position, it stops and calls me, and I sort it out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's half machine and half puzzle. When an autonomous rig stops, I've got to work out why, from the drill logs or by walking out to it. What wears me out is being away from Tomás, my partner, and missing Sunday Mass at home every second week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine by me, and I'd mean it. At camp I'd joke that the driverless drills still need a babysitter, and that's me. I'd probably post a short video of the rigs, because people at church think I work in a sci-fi film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays just as it is, and I like it. The autonomous drills are already here and they're not going anywhere, plateau or no plateau. So I keep being the person who knows both the manual rig and the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my roster and keep using AI every day to write my shift handover notes and check drill logs. I'd keep putting 500 a month into shares, on top of the four months of costs Tomás and I have saved. And I'd sign up for the next automation supervisor course when it opens, just because I want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite content. I'd be happy with that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How exactly does AI help with the handover notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I type in what happened, which rig stopped, why, how long it was down, and it turns it into a tidy handover for the next shift. Before AI, I spent forty minutes after every twelve-hour shift on paperwork; now it's ten, and that's thirty minutes more sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about home? Is there pressure there, even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás is a diesel mechanic on a different mine, on the opposite roster some months, which is hard. We want a baby in two or three years, and one of us will have to stop flying in and out. That's the real pressure on us, more than any AI.

say: She'd say **fine by me** and joke that driverless drills still need a babysitter.
She'd post a **short video** of the rigs for people at church.
think: The **autonomous drills** are already here, plateau or not.
She stays the person who knows **both the manual rig** and the screen.
do: Keep using **AI daily** for handover notes and checking drill logs.
Keep putting **500 a month** into shares on top of four months saved.
Sign up for the next **automation supervisor** course when it opens.
feel: **Calm** and content; she'd be happy in this world.
S0.quote: Before AI, I spent forty minutes after every twelve-hour shift on paperwork; now it's ten, and that's thirty minutes more sleep.
fieldNote: She already works **beside autonomous drills**, so she treats them as normal, not a threat.
AI saves her real time on **handover notes**, and she counts the gain in sleep.
Her true pressure is **family timing**: a baby in two or three years means one of them stops flying.

steps.text: Keep writing shift handovers and checking drill logs with AI
Put 500 a month into shares with Tomás
Keep working the eight-on, six-off drill roster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for the company and good for anyone willing to learn, and I'd say it without apologising. At camp some of the older drillers would roll their eyes. Online I'd share what courses are worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job is bigger than people think. If AI starts planning the drill patterns, one person watches six drills instead of two, and there won't be three of us. That person could be me, if I'm quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be that one person: I'd ask my superintendent, Graham, for the automation supervisor course this year, and I'd learn the new diagnosis software inside out. I'd keep the share savings going but add another month of cash, to get to five months. And I'd start looking at a part-time diploma in mining automation, about two years online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more alert than scared. It's like a new rig arriving: I want to be the first one trained on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there won't be three of you. How do you feel about the company cutting people that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's how business works, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. A company should run the mine the best way it can. But the company owes people a fair go at the training, and I'd say that to Graham's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the drillers who don't want to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start now, while there's time, and not to wait for the government to fix it. My dad was a fitter who taught himself hydraulics from library books. Nobody handed him anything, and nobody should expect it.

say: She'd say it's good for anyone **willing to learn**, without apologising.
Online she'd share which **courses** are worth doing.
think: The **thinking side** of her job is bigger than people think.
AI could let one person watch **six drills**, and that might be her, but not three of them.
do: Ask for the **automation supervisor** course this year.
Learn the new **diagnosis software** inside out and build savings to five months.
Look into a two-year online **automation diploma**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more alert than scared, like waiting to be first trained on a new rig.
S1.quote: If AI starts planning the drill patterns, one person watches six drills instead of two, and there won't be three of us.
fieldNote: She sees her job as more **thinking work** than outsiders assume, so Steady Disruption reaches her early.
She accepts **company cuts** as business but insists on a fair go at training.
Her model is her **self-taught father**, and she distrusts waiting on government.

steps.text: Ask superintendent Graham for the automation supervisor course
Learn the new rig diagnosis software inside out
Add a month of cash savings to reach five months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have every right to use it, but they'd better bring their people with them. At church I'd say we need to look after families, not just wait for a cheque. Online I'd probably post less, because people get nasty about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job gets hit twice. In 2028 the AI does the watching and the diagnosing, which is half of what I do, and around 2031 the robots do the hands-on fixing out at the rigs. So I don't really get the three-year gap that a pure hands-on worker gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the automation diploma straight away, nights on my off-weeks, and aim at the jobs that build and commission these systems, not run them. I'd pause the share buying and build cash to six months. And I'd talk to Tomás about him staying in diesel, because the robots break and he'll be fixing them longer than I'll be watching them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I'd rather have a list than lie there worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With all that going on, what happens to the baby plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably bring it forward, honestly, and have the baby sooner, with Tomás's job as the steadier one. I'd want our family started before everything shifts, not after. My mum would say God's timing, not the robots', and she'd have a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning time change about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm honest. Two years is too short to build a whole new skill. But I'd rather try and land halfway than sit still and land nowhere.

say: She'd say companies **have the right**, but must bring their people with them.
She'd talk at church about **looking after families**, and post less online.
think: Her job is **hit twice**: AI takes watching and diagnosing in 2028.
Robots take the **hands-on fixing** around 2031, so she misses the full three-year gap.
do: Start the **automation diploma** at once, studying in her off-weeks.
Pause share buying and build cash to **six months**.
Encourage Tomás to stay in **diesel repair**, the longer-lasting job.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy-anxious, preferring a to-do list to lying awake.
S2.quote: Two years is too short to build a whole new skill. But I'd rather try and land halfway than sit still and land nowhere.
fieldNote: She spotted that a **mixed job** gets hit at both dates, not just the later one.
She'd **have the baby sooner**, leaning on her partner's hands-on job as the steadier income.
Her **faith** frames the timing: her mother's "God's timing" line clearly carries weight.

steps.text: Start the online automation diploma in her off-weeks
Pause share buying and build cash to six months
Plan the baby sooner, relying on Tomás's diesel job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and nobody should waste it. I'd tell the younger ones at camp to pick a course this year. I'd keep it positive, because panic never helped anyone drill a straight hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same double hit as the fast one, just later: the screen work goes around 2031 and the hands-on work around 2034. But five years is long enough to finish a diploma and get a few years in a new role. I'd be 32 when the first part lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the two-year diploma next year and keep my roster. By 2029 I'd apply for commissioning jobs, the people who set up new automated fleets at other mines. I'd keep the shares going at 300 instead of 500 and keep five months of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. It feels like a long shift where you know when knock-off is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the baby fit in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably after the diploma, so around 2029, which is a bit later than I'd like. Tomás wants to wait until one of us is off the flights. I'd rather not wait forever, but I'd rather the baby has a parent at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't setting up these systems helping to replace the people you work with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty of people would say I'm helping put people out of work, setting up the machines. Someone's going to set up the machines, and I'd rather it's someone who has actually stood at the rig in forty-degree heat. That way it gets done properly.

say: She'd call five years **fair warning** and tell young workers to pick a course this year.
She'd stay **positive**, because panic never helped anyone drill a straight hole.
think: She faces the same **double hit**, later: screen work around 2031, hands-on around 2034.
Five years is enough to **finish a diploma** and work in a new role.
do: Start the **two-year diploma** next year while keeping her roster.
Apply for **commissioning jobs** setting up automated fleets by 2029.
Cut share buying to **300 a month** and keep five months of cash.
feel: **Uneasy** but with a plan, like a long shift with a known finish time.
S3.quote: Someone's going to set up the machines, and I'd rather it's someone who has actually stood at the rig in forty-degree heat.
fieldNote: She **owns the tension** of building the systems that replace drillers, and defends it.
The baby waits until **around 2029**, after the diploma, to her mild frustration.
Extra time turns her plan into a **career move**: commissioning automated fleets elsewhere.

steps.text: Start the two-year automation diploma next year
Apply for commissioning jobs on automated fleets by 2029
Keep buying shares at 300 a month
Wait until about 2029 to start a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and I'd say it to everyone. At camp I'd be the one handing out course brochures. Some of them would tease me for it, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best one for me. The screen work goes around 2036 and the hands-on work around 2039, and by then I'd have a diploma, a few years of commissioning work, and maybe a family. I'd be one of the people setting it up, not one of the people it lands on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the roster and the share savings at 500 a month. I'd do the diploma over the next two to three years at a comfortable pace, and Tomás and I would have the baby in about two years, like we planned. One of us would come off fly-in fly-out by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. It's a long runway, and I like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had children in that world, what would you want for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids to work hard and learn a trade, like my dad did, and then add whatever the new tools are. Not one or the other. And I'd want them close to family and the church, whatever the machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the slow version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who say "I'll deal with it when it comes," because ten years makes them comfortable. I've got a mate on the crew, Darren, who's said that about everything for five years. In this picture he'd still be saying it in 2035.

say: She'd call ten years **a gift** and say so to everyone.
At camp she'd hand out **course brochures**, and accept the teasing.
think: Screen work goes around **2036** and hands-on around 2039.
By then she'd be **setting it up**, not the one it lands on.
do: Keep the roster and **500 a month** in shares.
Finish the **diploma** over two to three years at a comfortable pace.
Have the **baby** in about two years, with one parent off fly-in fly-out.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, because she likes a long runway.
S4.quote: I'd be one of the people setting it up, not one of the people it lands on.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets her **traditional plans** and career moves fit together neatly.
She worries about **comfortable colleagues** like Darren who always say they'll deal with it later.
She wants future children to have **a trade first**, then the new tools.

steps.text: Keep the eight-on, six-off drill roster
Keep buying shares at 500 a month
Finish the automation diploma over two to three years
Have a baby in about two years with Tomás

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job gets hit at both ends and there's no time to finish anything. What would help is companies paying for real automation training, with time off the roster to do it, and hiring their own drillers first for the new jobs. Not handouts, just a fair start line.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and for me it matters. Whatever happens with the machines, my faith stays put. A robot can take my rig, but it can't take who I am on a Sunday.

headlineQuote: A robot can take my rig, but it can't take who I am on a Sunday.
portrait: Rosa is 27 and works **fly-in fly-out** on an iron ore drill crew, running one rig and watching two driverless ones.
She uses **AI every day** for handover notes and drill logs, and invests 500 a month in shares.
She's traditional on faith and family, and believes in **training, not handouts**, while accepting companies' right to automate.
She sees her job as **hit twice** under fast AGI, because watching rigs is thinking work.
She plans an **automation diploma** and commissioning work, and a baby with Tomás, timed to each scenario.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her mixed job is hit at both ends with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid automation training** with time off the roster.
Hiring their **own drillers first** for the new automation jobs.
